item.title: 3Dtrees.earth: community research infrastructure for tree and forest analysis using close-range LiDAR data
item.description: arXiv:2610.37803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: From individual trees to forest stands, three-dimensional structure shapes carbon, water, and energy flows, habitat conditions, and resource availability. Yet tree and forest structural attributes remain difficult to assess consistently across space and time. Close-range LiDAR (light detection and ranging) records detailed 3D structure from branches and trees to forest plots, including trees outside forests. However, broader reuse is constrained when data, acquisition context, processing, computation, and access conditions are maintained separately. We present 3Dtrees.earth, an operational community research infrastructure that brings close-range LiDAR datasets, analysis tools, and computing resources together while linking original observations to their metadata and processing outputs. As of 23 October 2026, the platform comprised 2,760 datasets, including 2,481 publicly visible datasets. These point cloud datasets span 46 countries on all six inhabited continents and include terrestrial, mobile, and uncrewed aerial laser scanning. Users can contribute and discover datasets, run standardized processing workflows on shared computing infrastructure, inspect point clouds and model predictions in the browser, and access data and processing outputs together with citation information. Workflows combine rule-based and machine-learning methods, with tools updated as methods advance. Outputs include raster products, individual-tree and semantic segmentation, and tree- and stand-level metrics. Original point clouds and processing records are retained, enabling reprocessing with improved tools while preserving provenance. With broader coverage, curation, and validation, this shared resource could extend individual surveys into a basis for model evaluation and benchmarking, cross-site synthesis, calibration and validation of larger-scale Earth observation products, and macroecological analysis.

item.title: Integrated data, metadata, and paradata management system for 3D Digital Cultural Heritage objects: Workflow automation, federated authentication, and publication
item.description: arXiv:2610.38585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The complexity of high-quality 3D digitised cultural heritage objects creates challenges for existing data management systems as they need to develop metadata management and processing capabilities to provide semantic insight into the interconnectivity of data that constitutes cultural heritage objects. To address these challenges, we propose a global federated authentication and authorisation mechanism, a data and metadata management system, and an integrated engine for designing and executing automated workflows that facilitate the processing of both data and metadata. The solution is evaluated with three distinct 3D digitised cultural objects and presents the complete process from data upload to cultural heritage object publication
item.dc:creator: Michal Orzechowski, Lukasz Opiola, Ignacio Lamata Martinez, Marinos Ioannides, Panayiotis N. Panayiotou, Lukasz Dutka, Renata G. Slota, Jacek Kitowski

item.title: Guidance List for repOrting Bibliometric AnaLyses (GLOBAL): A Reporting Guideline Informed by a Two-Round Modified Delphi Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.38748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background: Despite the growth of bibliometric analyses, few studies offer guidance on how to report them, resulting in a lack of research transparency and completeness. To address this gap, we developed the Guidance List for the repOrting of Bibliometric AnaLyses (GLOBAL). Methods: An initial list of items for the GLOBAL was generated through a scoping review and refined through a modified two-round Delphi, as recommended by the EQUATOR Network. The guideline was finalized through a pilot test, where participants assessed their manuscripts using the checklist and Elaboration and Explanation (E&E) document, which outlines item expectations and provides examples. Results: The scoping review resulted in 32 items. In Round 1, 24 items reached consensus and thematic content analysis resulted in one additional item. This item, along with the eight items that did not reach consensus, were discussed in detail in Round 2. During the in-person meeting, one item was split into two, totalling ten voting items. Eight out of ten items reached consensus, five for inclusion and three for exclusion. Conclusions: The finalized 28-item GLOBAL (and its accompanying E&E document) provides users with a framework to report bibliometric analyses, aimed at promoting high-quality reporting of bibliometric analyses in scholarly literature.

item.title: Behind the Paper Explosion: Author Growth and Widening Gaps in Computer Science
item.description: arXiv:2610.39831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth of computer science (CS) papers increases the work needed to review research and find relevant studies. The growing use of AI tools in scientific writing makes it increasingly important to identify the authors behind this growth. Previous studies have tracked publication growth and followed researchers' careers, documenting the increasing number of authors and the many researchers who publish only briefly. However, annual averages of papers per author reflect different sets of researchers and may hide changes among the same authors. This study addresses this gap by linking individual changes to overall CS paper growth using arXiv, DBLP, and conference submission records for 2010-2025. With each paper divided equally among its authors, the total paper count equals the number of authors multiplied by their average papers per author. This relationship provides a decomposition of the two contributions of paper growth. This decomposition attributes nearly all growth in CS paper volume to an increase in the number of publishing authors. The analysis of author numbers further distinguishes expansion through new and returning arXiv authors from the replacement of authors no longer publishing there. Changes in who publishes also affect the average, motivating comparisons of the same authors over time within groups with similar past paper counts. This comparison identifies substantial replacement within the growing author group. New authors average fewer papers under this counting method, keeping the overall average nearly unchanged despite increases among authors who published in both years. Moreover, statistics show that these increases are uneven, with widening gaps even among authors who previously published similar numbers of papers. These findings provide insights into peer review, community participation, researcher evaluation, and equity within the CS community.
item.dc:creator: Jiayi Li, Bowen Niu, Bingsheng He, Zhaomin Wu

item.title: The FlightFinder Occurrence Corpus: harmonising 128 aviation-safety source codes into one deduplicated cross-national accident dataset
item.description: arXiv:2610.37671v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: National aviation-investigation databases are deep but territorial; global compilations such as the Aviation Safety Network and the Bureau of Aircraft Accidents Archives are hand-curated, apply their own inclusion thresholds, and publish no per-record lineage. The FlightFinder Occurrence Corpus harmonizes 279,485 occurrences and 131,882 attached narratives from 128 source codes -- national accident-investigation authorities, occurrence-reporting systems and four global compilations. Records are mapped into one schema; each normalized record reduces to exactly one key from an ordered ladder -- event signature, registration and date, rounded position and date, or source and native identifier -- so a missing field never creates a link, and the key is the occurrence identifier. Records the ladder cannot reach are scored in a blocked pass into an explicit merge table and applied only within an automatically approved score band or after a person confirms them. Field conflicts follow a documented source ranking; one provenance row per contributing source -- its native identifier and URL -- is retained, with attribution and licence terms per source code. Linkage error is measured on five adjudicated samples totalling 200 pairs. A recorded uniform random draw of 60 from the 3,441 merges the automatic band applies as it ships found no error; the exact two-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson upper bound on its false-merge rate is 6.0%, or 205 pairs. The measured error covers the scored band only; the ladder's deterministic joins are not adjudicated. The corpus has no exposure denominators and inherits the under-reporting of its sources. It is offered as a base for cross-national safety statistics, source-disagreement studies and narrative text mining; a frozen, DOI-referenced snapshot accompanies the live API.
item.dc:creator: Denys Kolomiiets

item.title: Ignore the Writing: A Proposal for Peer Review in the Age of AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.38062v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The written paper has long stood in as proof of work: a fluent, well-structured manuscript was taken as evidence that good research lay behind it. Generative AI has broken that link. Polished manuscripts now cost nothing to produce, submissions are outgrowing what reviewers can absorb, and venues are turning to AI for help. The logical endpoint is a loop where AI writes the papers and AI reviews them. We argue that this loop is survivable, but only if it is given a reward function, and that human reviewing effort should become that reward function. We propose that submissions should consist of a 1500-word brief plus an unlimited, machine-verifiable appendix. Human reviewers judge whether a pursuit is worthwhile, models verify the experimental record in the appendix, and human curation decides where the field goes next.
item.dc:creator: Vassilis Kostakos

item.title: Beyond fabrication: Misattributed numbers in papers written by AI research agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.38691v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Verifying numerical claims in research written by AI agents is an important but challenging problem. Recent benchmarks show that many agent-written papers fail integrity checks, but such verdicts, often produced by a single LLM judge, identify failure without explaining its nature, and existing checks either test a paper for internal consistency or test whether a reported value appears somewhere in an agent's output. We re-analyze all 540 released judgments from a recent public benchmark of AI research agents (nine agents, fifteen open research problems) and manually label 256 numerical claims from 18 submissions. Failures concentrate on alignment between the paper and the underlying work rather than overt cheating, and about four in five unsupported claims correspond to values in the agent's own files that come from the wrong experiment, metric, or run. We introduce a deterministic claim-to-evidence checker that scores whether the surrounding context identifies the claimed result and calibrates each claim against numerical decoys. With its rules fixed before labeling, it certifies claims with over 90% precision against blinded annotators (78 of 85; Cohen's kappa = 0.89), while verifying only a subset of claims; most claims it cannot verify are nevertheless traceable, so failure to verify is not evidence of falsehood. An LLM verifier given the same evidence recovers more traceable claims but accepts about three times as many misattributed ones, so the two are best used together. Applied to 99 submissions, the checker reveals large differences in traceability across agents, and a second judge from a different vendor preserves the official agent ranking while passing twice as many papers. These findings motivate provenance-first auditing of AI-produced research.
item.dc:creator: Mosab Alfaqeeh, Omar Hourani, Muath Hourani, Hashem Alfaqeeh

item.title: Rebuilding a Field's Open-Problem Catalog from the Literature: A Two-Layer Knowledge Graph, and Why Status Must Stay Proposed
item.description: arXiv:2610.39641v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A research field records its open problems in surveys, keynotes and community reports. Those are prose, written every few years, and nobody can ask them who works on a problem now or whether it was settled last year. We argue the problems should be data, and we build the system that makes them so: a hand-curated problem layer carried in unchanged, under an evidence layer rebuilt from a bibliographic index, joined by typed, provenance-carrying links in one graph database and queryable from one language. A language model does four jobs -- per-paper extraction, catalog grounding, per-paper status verdict, and idea generation -- each constrained to a candidate set so out-of-set answers are refused rather than stored. We report a study on two curated catalogs, database research (1,053 problems) and AI research (1,000 problems), each with a prior catalog-only graph. The rebuilt graph answers every question the catalog-only graph answered -- 47 of 47 on databases, 34 of 35 on AI -- plus questions the catalog-only graph refused: recent workers, untouched problems, methods tried, and outside papers bearing on a problem (336 problems, 770 works on databases). The capability we most wanted does not survive its own audit. Of 41 solves and refutes verdicts hand-checked against the papers, 9 are correct, 30 partly correct and 2 wrong; no refutes verdict (0 of 34) disproves an open problem, and only 1 of 7 solves closes the central question. We report that failure in full and draw the design conclusion: a status change must be proposed with its evidence and never applied, making the human reviewer part of the architecture. We close with the data-engineering problems this raises: entity resolution across curated and harvested layers, verifying model status claims, freshness under source quotas, and evaluation without ground truth.
item.dc:creator: Madhulatha Mandarapu, Sandeep Kunkunuru

item.title: Large scientific teams are more, not less, disruptive
item.description: arXiv:2610.07329v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern science has moved decisively toward larger and more collaborative research teams. Yet an influential 2019 study reported that small teams are more disruptive than large teams, a conclusion difficult to reconcile with both the well-known trend toward increasing collaboration and the disproportionately large teams behind widely recognized disruptive research, such as work that has been awarded Nobel Prizes. Here we show that the reported disruptive advantage of small teams is largely an artifact of measurement rather than a fact about teams. Analyzing about 60 million scientific publications, we find that larger teams cite more references and that the standard disruption index declines mechanically as reference lists lengthen. Equalizing reference-count distributions across team sizes reverses the negative gradient within the index's own framework. Evaluating each paper against one reference at a time yields a reference-robust measure that distinguishes recognized breakthroughs from ordinary papers more sharply and more consistently than the standard disruption index across six independently curated benchmarks, including the Nobel Prize. Under this validated measurement, scientific disruption increases with team size across four scientific domains and in every decade from the 1970s to the 2010s. For scientific publications, we conclude that larger teams are more, not less, disruptive.
item.dc:creator: Junming Huang, Yu Xie

item.title: FISH Omics Format: a standard enabling FAIR chromatin tracing data sharing across repositories
item.description: arXiv:2508.13255v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In recent years, multiplexed Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH) or FISH-omics methods have rapidly expanded, enabling the quantification of chromatin organization in single cells, often in conjunction with measurements of RNAs and proteins. These approaches have deepened our understanding of how 3D chromosome architecture relates to transcriptional activity and cell states in health and disease. Despite these advances, results from Chromatin Tracing FISH-omics experiments remain challenging to share, reuse, and analyze due to the absence of standardized data exchange specifications. Building on the release of microscopy metadata standards, we introduce the FISH Omics Format-Chromatin Tracing (FOF-CT), a community-developed standard for processed results from diverse imaging modalities. We describe the FOF-CT file format and present a curated collection of datasets deposited in the 4D Nucleome Data Portal and the OME Image Data Resource (IDR). We also highlight their potential for reuse, integration, and modeling by outlining example analysis pipelines and illustrating biological insights enabled by standardized, FAIR-compliant Chromatin Tracing datasets. FOF-CT natively represents both ball-and-stick and volumetric Chromatin Tracing data, unifying the two modalities within a single, modular table-based architecture (FOF-bas-CT and FOF-vol-CT, respectively).

item.title: The Costs of Early-career Disciplinary Pivots: Evidence from Ph.D. Admissions
item.description: arXiv:2603.22805v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Science often advances when researchers pivot from one discipline to another and import new ideas. However, for established researchers, such pivots are associated with fewer publications and citations. Here, we investigate pivoting at the beginning of a research career--doctoral admissions--when the benefits of importing ideas might outweigh the switching costs. Analyzing 171,347 PhD applications at a large research university from 2013 to 2023, we measured the semantic distance between each applicant's prior degree and target program. Applicants who pivot further had lower undergraduate grades and, controlling for academic and demographic predictors, lower admission chances: the average pivot corresponds to a 5.3% lower admission probability (0.80 percentage points). Among enrollees, the average pivoter takes longer to graduate than non-pivoters, with a 10.7% lower graduation hazard, and similar publication and citation counts on average and at the tails. Our results suggest that pivoting at the outset of research careers, even if it benefits research communities, comes with significant costs to individuals.
item.dc:creator: Sidney Xiang, Nicholas David, Dallas Card, Wenhao Sun, Daniel M Romero, Misha Teplitskiy

item.title: Real-World Evaluation of an AI Agent Drafting Translational Impact Summaries
item.description: arXiv:2607.16989v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Introduction. Clinical and Translational Science Award (CTSA) programs must document their scholars' research impact, but assembling each scholar's record by hand takes staff an estimated 15 hours and does not scale to a full cohort. An artificial intelligence (AI) agent could serve as a tool to gather scholar data across platforms and disciplines. Methods. We built a human-in-the-loop AI agent that assembles a dossier of sourced evidence for each scholar and drafts one-sentence Translational Science Benefits Model (TSBM) impact summaries for staff review. We evaluated it in the impact-reporting workflow of one CTSA hub across 10 career-development (KL2/K12) scholars. Two evaluation staff independently coded all 507 findings as accept, edit, or reject; the primary measure was the unanimous usable rate, defined as the share both accepted or edited. Results. Both reviewers accepted or edited 81.7% of the agent's findings. Reviewers each spent a median of 14 minutes per scholar, replacing an estimated 15 hours of manual assembly. Inter-rater agreement was moderate (Cohen's kappa 0.43 on the usable-versus-reject decision). A profile discovery study found the agent's recall close to human search. The agent's impact evidence spanned all four TSBM domains, and about a third of the reviewed findings fell in non-scholarly categories that routine processes tend to miss. Reviewers rated synthesis accuracy 4.5 and usefulness 4.8 on a 5-point scale. Conclusions. A human-in-the-loop AI agent can serve as the first-pass author of a scholar's impact record, shifting staff from collecting and writing to reviewing, and making cohort-scale impact reporting feasible.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Arvan, Amber E. Osterholt, Bailee Rue, Yuvaneswaren R. Sureshbabu, Krishna R. Patel, Rebecca T. Feinstein, Bethany C. Bray, Niranjan S. Karnik
